Phenomenology studies the development of self-consciousness, and self-consciousness finds its most accurate expression in philosophy. Phenomenology therefore also appears as a kind of “history” of philosophy.
But it “periodizes,” “schematizes,” and “idealizes” that history. If one prefers, it understands the philosophers it studies more fully and accurately than they understood themselves.
When it speaks on their behalf, it therefore says what they could have said, given their historical conditions, but for one “accidental” reason or another did not actually say.
The phenomenological history of philosophy, which forms part of Phenomenology, thus differs fundamentally from ordinary or “scholarly” history. It is a philosophical “history” of philosophy.
179) Phenomenology shows why, under certain historical conditions, a human being capable of writing it can emerge—even though that “possibility” may never actually be used.
But it cannot explain why it is written in this particular year by this particular person: by Hegel, Kojevnikov, “Sidorov,” or “Petrov.”
Everything belonging to its author’s “personal life” is therefore left aside: everything that distinguishes Hegel or Kojevnikov from their contemporaries.
In principle, Phenomenology can be written by anyone, provided the necessary historical conditions exist.
And this is why, in principle, it can “turn any reader into a philosopher.”

In reality, the phenomenological method he supposedly discovered—a purely descriptive method—was no different from the method Hegel used throughout his philosophy and especially in his Phenomenology.

188) This is particularly awkward because, in saying it, I immediately put myself in opposition not only to Hegel but also to many representatives of Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist thought.
As for Hegel, it could be shown that he discovered dialectic through his study of history and only afterward applied it to the natural world.
Indeed, all the definitions he gives of dialectic make sense only when applied to human reality.
In his anthropological writings, dialectic produced brilliant results. In his philosophy of nature, by contrast, it led him into complete disaster.
Historically, Hegel’s mistake is easy to understand.

He made a philosophically revolutionary discovery when he recognized the dialectical structure of existence, something classical philosophy had never known. But it was difficult for him to carry out a second revolution at the same time: to abandon the traditional ontological monism according to which everything that exists ultimately has one and the same structure.
Having recognized the “dialectical character” of existence, Hegel therefore concluded that everything that exists is dialectical.
Psychologically, this is perfectly understandable. When someone makes a new discovery, he naturally tends to overestimate it and tries to apply it in areas where it does not really apply.
Marx, for his part, was initially interested only in the human world. Hegelian dialectic struck and convinced him precisely because it allowed him to understand this human world of history.
By Marx’s time, Hegel’s Naturphilosophie had long since been consigned to oblivion. When Marx spoke about Hegel, he simply was not thinking about it.

The very fact that he gave his doctrine the title “dialectical” or “historical materialism”—although in our terminology it would be better called “realism”—shows that for him historicity and dialecticity coincide.
In his own independent work, meaning work not dependent on Engels, Marx generally does not deal with the natural world as such. In practice, therefore, he does not apply dialectic to nature.
Nevertheless, in principle he does not reject Hegel’s position that dialectic is present in both the human and natural worlds.

It seems to me that Marx was influenced here by Engels, who not only accepted Hegel’s position without qualification but also made the rather unfortunate attempt to create a “dialectical science” of the natural world, influencing Marx in the same direction.
I will not examine here why this happened.
I will only say that Engels’s philosophical authority should not be exaggerated.
He was unquestionably an important and talented man. But it is simply impossible to place him on the same level as Hegel and Marx—or Lenin and Stalin.

In general, the more deeply and completely we come to understand Marx, the easier it becomes to see how greatly Engels simplifies the thought of his extraordinary friend and sometimes even distorts it.

Indeed, one can argue that it was Engels in particular who made the Social Democratic distortion of Marx possible—a distortion characteristic of contemporary Western thought—and in this respect he bears a heavy responsibility.
Engels is especially responsible for allowing Hegel’s mistaken ideas about a supposedly “dialectical Naturphilosophie” to survive within Marxist and even Leninist-Stalinist thought.
It should be recognized once and for all that no “dialectical” theory exists, or has ever existed, in any field of scientific knowledge of the real world.
Where such theories have appeared—as, for example, in Engels—they have produced nothing but confusion and failure.

Attempts to force physicists, chemists, biologists, and others to think “dialectically” have therefore not only achieved nothing. One can hardly count as a success the “dialectical” prefaces placed before books whose actual contents contain no dialectic at all.
These attempts have also helped spread among scientists a general scepticism toward dialectic itself.
189) Before the Greeks, people had a “magical” picture of the world which, if one likes, had a “dialectical” character.
Conversely, the attempts by Hegel and others to apply dialectic to the scientific study of nature always led to purely “magical” theories.
The Greeks discovered the non-dialectical character of the natural world.
But they themselves were then carried away by their discovery and extended it to the whole world, including human beings.
Magic was mistaken precisely because it humanized, or anthropologized, nature. The Greeks corrected this mistake.
But by then turning human beings into something purely worldly or natural—by cosmologizing them—they went to the opposite extreme.
Hegel corrected the Greek mistake but went too far himself and, so to speak, returned to magic.
In other words, instead of finding a synthesis of the Greek antithesis and the magical thesis, he simply moved back from the Greek antithesis to the magical thesis.
The true synthesis consists precisely in interpreting human beings “magically” while speaking about nature in the Greek way.
Of course, the “magic” defended by this synthesis—that is, dialectic—is fundamentally different from real magic as it appeared in the original thesis.
But the two do have something in common.

191) One can say that the Greeks discovered the category of “identity,” while Hegel discovered the category of “negativity,” and with it dialectic in general.
There can be little doubt that these are two of the most important discoveries in the entire history of philosophy. It is therefore worth examining them in somewhat greater detail.
Before the emergence of Greek philosophy, a “magical” view or understanding of the world seems to have been widespread everywhere.
This “magic” already taught people to distinguish the “essence” or “nature” of a thing from its outward appearance, and its “essential” qualities from its “inessential” ones.
Many different names were invented for this “essence.” Modern sociology adopted the Polynesian word “mana.”
The magical view therefore held that we must distinguish between a thing’s visible appearance, which has no “essential” value, and its invisible “mana,” which constitutes the thing’s true essence.
Magic itself consists in knowing how to act directly and practically on this “mana,” and thereby gain control over the outward appearance of things.
Above all, it was important to know how to name the mana correctly and act upon it through a special form of speech suited to it: a “spell.”
In this sense, the magical view of the world was already scientific.
Second, it held that knowledge of the essence gives us power over the thing itself.
The contemporary scientist reasons in exactly the same way. Knowledge of the “essence” of gold gives the chemist “power” over objects made of gold.
And this knowledge is expressed above all in the practical ability to name that essence correctly—to know its “formula.”
Yet there is an essential difference between magic and genuine science.
